Fast tier because cache-control gives a 300s TTL, and 15 minutes sits above that floor with headroom for edge age skew. ACTIVE since 2026-08-31, and what changed is the denylist rather than the extractor. This source sat pending while its extractor was already verified against two live 5.2 MB captures minutes apart: 1,846 projected record tuples, byte-unequal bodies, equal projections. It was blocked upstream of the predicate, at the health check, because the live leaderboard carries window.__CF$cv$params and that string was on the shared interstitial denylist. THAT MARKER WAS WRONG. It is set by Cloudflare's challenge-platform beacon, which loads on ordinary proxied 200s wherever JS Detections or Bot Fight Mode is enabled, so it marked "this site is behind Cloudflare" rather than "this response is a challenge", and every Cloudflare-fronted source was a potential false positive. Three live captures on 2026-08-31 settle the direction of the error: a real Cloudflare managed challenge (test/fixtures/trap-cf-challenge-udemy.html) carries NO __CF$cv$params at all, while three ordinary 200s that are not challenges (this leaderboard, crunchbase.com, and the neuron homepage in test/fixtures/trap-interstitial.html) each carry exactly one. It is replaced by cf_chl_opt and /cdn-cgi/challenge-platform/h/, which appear in all three live challenge captures, in zero archived captures and in zero of the non-challenge pages; test/health.test.ts sweeps every marker against every stored capture so the next one added has to clear the same bar. Predicate is extracted, not bytes, because two reviewers measured three per-request volatile regions independently and hours apart: a provisional userId UUIDv7 whose embedded ms timestamp decodes to the fetch instant, a 37 to 41 key posthogFlags map that re-rolls because the visitor is anonymous, and the __CF$cv$params blob itself, which carries the response's own cf-ray and clock and so changes on every response by construction. Masking only the first leaves the bodies unequal, so the predicate would fire every run and commit 5.2 MB forever into a history that is never rewritten, and a mask keyed on flag names rots as arena ships experiments. The projection is the (publicName, displayName, rating, votes) tuples behind a 500-record floor, because the payload is an undocumented framework shape and a silent drop to zero would report no change for ever. Size is per-request volatile (5,266,753 and 5,266,756 observed on 2026-08-31), so minBytes is half the smaller 2026-08-26 observation and no fixed size is asserted. Freshness content/30 rather than the usual 90: codename reveals are the entire point, so a quiet month means the extractor broke rather than that the industry stopped shipping. timeoutS 120 for a 5.2 MB body. Activated after a double dry run in which the second consecutive run committed nothing.

Predicate is extracted over sitemapDated, not bytes. Measured twice: two fetches four seconds apart on 2026-08-26 differed in 24 of 516 lastmod values with the loc set identical, and two fetches four minutes apart on 2026-08-31 differed in 25 of 522, the values oscillating backwards, which is two live edge-cache generations rather than a rebuild. A bytes predicate would commit 68 KB of that oscillation on every run into a history that is never rewritten. sitemapDated rather than sitemapLoc is the load-bearing choice: keying on the loc set alone reduces this source to add and remove detection, and its per-URL lastmod is the only thing that makes an EDIT to a page that already exists detectable at all. sitemapDated keeps every lastmod except those shared by three or more URLs at the same millisecond, which is the build stamp. The oscillating values all share one stamp; a real single-page edit does not. Activated 2026-08-31 after a double dry run in which the second consecutive run committed nothing.

The forecasting artifact. 13,410 bytes for the .md twin against 1,006,482 for the HTML page, which is why the .md URL is the archived one; minBytes is half the 13,410. contentType text because a markdown parse check is exactly as vacuous as a plain text one, so the canary carries the health check here. Non-numeric families exist (claude-fable-5, claude-mythos-preview), so no claude-(opus|sonnet|haiku)-N regex anywhere downstream. Eight or more further tables follow the master one.

Predicate is extracted over sitemapLoc, the loc set only. This sitemap is not static: cache-control is public, max-age=0, must-revalidate and cf-cache-status is DYNAMIC. It is rebuilt several times a day, rewriting about 100 lastmod values per rebuild independent of any content change, so a bytes predicate would commit 617 KB of build noise every run into a history that is never rewritten. This is the same treatment already given to platform.claude.com/sitemap.xml. Unlike anthropic-sitemap the loc set is the whole signal here, because the per-URL lastmod is rewritten wholesale rather than per edit, so there is no edit signal in it to preserve. retries 3 rather than the usual 2 because a curl (35) connection reset was observed against this host. Activated 2026-08-31 after a double dry run in which the second consecutive run committed nothing; the two probe bodies were in fact byte-identical, 4,973 locs each.

ACTIVE since 2026-08-31. THE WRITE-TIME CREDENTIAL GATE IN src/secrets.ts IS THE PROTECTION HERE, NOT DARKNESS. On 2026-08-31 this file carried an 84-character xai- credential, three times, as "apiKey": "xai-...", in xAI's own published llms.txt. GitHub push protection classified it as a live xAI API Key and refused the push, which is the only reason it never reached the archive. Push protection is not a control we get to rely on: it recognises only the formats it has partnered on, the next provider may use one it has never seen, and it fires after the bytes are already in a local commit. The gate runs between the change decision and the write, so a body carrying a credential is not written, not committed, and recorded as a hold while the run exits zero. A hold is deliberately not a failure: the source is healthy, the fetch worked, the predicate saw a real change, and the provider made the mistake, so a daily failure email about it would only teach an operator to mute the channel. Never resolve this with the push-protection bypass link. Re-measured 2026-08-31: the credential is still published, so this source is expected to sit HELD on every run until xAI takes it down, and meta/status.json names the hold with the pattern, the count and the byte offset and never with the credential itself. On the predicate: bytes is wrong here because the file's markdown table rows re-permute per request, so it would commit 1.46 MB of pure permutation daily forever, and mask cannot express it because a reordering is not a maskable substring. The extracted predicate sorts within table blocks only, never the whole file, which would hide a legitimate section reorder; header and delimiter rows keep their positions, so a renamed column is still a change. The sorted md5 b92fafe614002915ea5a5b5e5be3060b reproduced across three independent captures hours apart while every raw md5 differed.

The repository is anomalyco/models.dev, not sst/models.dev. 20 entries, 20,239 bytes, no API rate limit, so minBytes is half the recorded size. The observed 20-entry window spanned 24m29s, so a daily poll loses commits and even a fast tier could; O3 resolves that with git fetch rather than a tier move, which is why this stays daily. freshness feed/7 rather than the incident feeds' 120 because this is an activity feed that cycles its whole window in under half an hour, so a week of silence means the feed or the repo is dead, not that the project is quiet. sizeBand widened to [0.4, 3.0] because a fixed count window of 20 commits sizes with how verbose the messages are, which is not a content integrity signal.

Predicate is mask, not bytes. 25 entries, all carrying published, newest 2026-08-24T20:26:21Z. Downstream must key on published and not updated: 16 of the 25 share a bulk backfill updated of 2026-08-14. The mask covers the feed-level updated element and nothing else. That line advances per cache generation while every entry stays byte-identical, and it has already produced seven commits whose entire content is one timestamp moving: commits 3a80c22 and 690dd60, 49 minutes apart, differ in that line alone across two 33,787-byte captures. The pattern is a negative lookbehind for an opening entry tag rather than an indentation match, so it selects the one updated element that precedes the first entry and can never reach an entry's own updated: measured on the archived body, 1 masked and all 25 entry updated elements left in place. freshness feed/120 because a provider with a genuinely good quarter publishes no incidents for 60+ days, and a daily failure mail for that is how alerting channels get muted; a stale feed is stale, not failed, and does not drive the exit code. minBytes is deliberately a stub catcher at 1,024 bytes, which an empty or error body cannot clear.

Predicate is extracted over atomStatus, not bytes. Measured 2026-08-26: six fetches gave two distinct md5s at an identical 92,282 bytes. Two things move per cache generation and neither is an incident. The feed-level updated re-stamps, and the affected-component list inside every entry is permuted, 493 differing runs across 15,600 bytes, while entry id order and set stay stable. atomStatus projects each entry's id, its updated, and its component list SORTED. Sorting kills the permutation while leaving a component APPEARING or VANISHING visible, which is the quiet withdrawal a status feed exists to leak; dropping the component list would be cheaper and would throw that away. The feed-level updated sits outside every entry and so is never read. This feed carries zero published elements, only updated, which is why freshness reads the entry-scoped date rather than the document-wide one. Activated 2026-08-31 after a double dry run in which the second consecutive run committed nothing.

Leaks-desk signal 2: an open-weights model cannot launch until its runtime support is upstreamed, so the pull request naming an architecture exists in public before any weights do. Probed live 2026-08-31: HTTP 200, 483,237 bytes, total_count 203, per_page=100 reaching back to 2024-09-20. The GitHub SEARCH API is a separate rate-limit bucket from the core REST API at 10 requests per minute unauthenticated, which one daily call does not come close to; the core bucket's 60 per hour is the tighter one and this endpoint does not use it. per_page is 100 rather than a smaller window because the merge transition is the whole point of the signal and a pull request that falls out of the created-desc window before it merges can never produce that event; 100 items is roughly six weeks on the busier of the two repositories. The query filters on title only, and deliberately loosely, because R3 puts normalization in the deriver: the archive holds the superset and src/derive/leaks.ts applies the `Add <Capitalized> model support` filter over it, so tightening the filter later is a code change rather than a hole in the history. The predicate is githubPulls and not bytes. What is measured and what is reasoned is kept apart here: two fetches 40 minutes apart on 2026-08-31 were BYTE IDENTICAL, so per-request volatility of the arena or openai-status kind is NOT claimed for this source. What moves is activity: every item carries an `updated_at` that advances on any comment or label, a `comments` count, a `reactions` block, a relevance `score`, and a feed-level `total_count` that moves as unrelated pull requests match the query. On a repository with 1,043 matching pull requests and daily traffic, a comment on any of the hundred in the window is a full-body commit under bytes and is not a model-support signal. Measured against the stored artifact: applying only those five field families plus a reversal of item order changes 483,237 bytes to 483,559 and the predicate reports unchanged, while flipping one merged_at from null to a date reports changed. githubPulls projects (number, title, state, merged_at) and nothing else. merged_at is projected because state cannot stand in for it: a closed pull request is abandoned or merged, and the search payload distinguishes the two, so keying on state alone would file an abandoned attempt and a landed runtime commit as one event. minBytes 200000 is under half the smallest observation because `body` is user-authored and its length dominates the payload size. minRecords 40 against 100 requested leaves headroom for a search API that returns short.

The second half of leaks-desk signal 2, and it is a separate source rather than a second query because the two repositories upstream on different clocks: vLLM has 1,043 all-time matches against transformers' 203, and its 100-item window reaches back six weeks where the transformers window reaches back two years. Probed live 2026-08-31: HTTP 200, 657,623 bytes, total_count 1043, newest item the same day. Predicate githubPulls, not bytes, for exactly the reasons written on transformers-pulls, and with the same care about what is measured: two fetches 40 minutes apart were byte identical, so the justification is activity-driven churn rather than per-request volatility. Measured against the stored artifact: comment-driven `updated_at`, `comments`, `reactions`, `score`, `total_count` and a reversed item order together move 657,623 bytes to 657,933 and the predicate reports unchanged, while one merged_at going non-null reports changed. The projection is (number, title, state, merged_at). Confirming a catch is a second, uncollected step by design: the deriver publishes the pull request as a confirmed artifact and never as a launch, because huggingface.co/api/models returning [] for the architecture name is evidence about a weights repository and not about the pull request, and merging the two into one sentence is the claim the copy rule forbids. minBytes 250000 is under half the observation for the same reason as transformers-pulls: `body` dominates. minRecords 40 against 100 requested.
